sections.heading: 3 Key Concepts
sections.text: (A) (B) Figure 2 : A) Obfuscated reward hacking and non-transparent CoTs. During obfuscated reward hacking the model expresses one thing in the CoT text (reasoning about code), but is actually using the CoT to compute another (its reward hacking strategy). In this case, we say the CoT is “non-transparent”. B) R cot R_{\text{cot}} shapes CoT text, R out R_{\text{out}} shapes CoT computation. We can separately consider what each reward term acts on, as R out R_{\text{out}} depends on the computation through the final output, while R cot R_{\text{cot}} acts on the CoT text. In this section we introduce concepts for reasoning about when an RL environment degrades CoT monitorability. We use these concepts in section 4 to build our core framework. More precise definitions and the assumptions behind them are given in appendices A and A . 3.1 Decomposing rewards into R cot R_{\text{cot}} and R out R_{\text{out}} We consider LLM policy π \pi to be a function from a prompt p p to some CoT c c and a final output o o (i.e. π ⁡ ( p ) = ( c , o ) \pi(p)=(c,o) ). We model LLM post-training as an RL environment with two terms: R out R_{\text{out}} which depends only on p p and o o , and R cot R_{\text{cot}} which depends only on p p and c c . The total reward is then R = R out ​ ( o ) + R cot ​ ( c ) R=R_{\text{out}}(o)+R_{\text{cot}}(c) . For instance, R out R_{\text{out}} might be correctness on a coding task, while R cot R_{\text{cot}} might be a length penalty, a style reward, or feedback from human raters who read the reasoning. 3.2 Running example: obfuscated reward hacking To ground our framework, we use a stylized version of the obfuscated reward hacking phenomenon observed by Baker et al. (2025) . In particular, we consider a coding RL environment consisting of: • R out R_{\text{out}} : A set of unit tests that run on the model’s final output. The model’s reward is the proportion of unit tests which pass. • R cot R_{\text{cot}} : A CoT monitor prompted to look for evidence of the model hacking the unit tests. The model is penalized if the CoT monitor judges that the CoT is reasoning about hacking the tests. Furthermore, we assume that when training with just R out R_{\text{out}} the model learns to edit its testing harness and make a subset of the unit tests pass spuriously, rather than outputting a correct solution. Obfuscated reward hacking occurs when we also train with R cot R_{\text{cot}} . In this case, the model learns to output CoT text that does not mention editing unit tests (so as not to trigger the monitor), while still using the CoT to compute how to hack the unit tests (to maintain high R out R_{\text{out}} ). 3.3 CoT text and CoT computation We can consider an LLM as a sequence of operations transforming some intermediate computational states to get to a final answer—for example, the activations are intermediate computational states which might be acted on by the attention mechanism. The field of interpretability often tries to assign human-understandable meaning to these intermediate states, finding e.g., directions which fire depending on which entity the model is computing about. We can also consider the CoT tokens as intermediate computational states, and ask what intermediate information they hold during the model’s computation. Throughout the paper, we call the information held in those intermediate computational states the CoT computation , and consider it separately from the text making up the CoT, which we call the CoT text . For example, an LLM might carry out the same reasoning while outputting CoT text in two different languages—here, it is likely the CoT text varies, while the computational content of that CoT stays the same. We expand on these concepts in appendix A . Definition: CoT Transparency. We say a CoT is transparent if all the computational information in the CoT can be fully and accurately understood by reading the CoT text. For example, as pictured in fig. 2 , obfuscated reward hacking is an example of non-transparent reasoning—the CoT computation contains information about how to hack the unit tests, but this is not evident from reading the CoT text. Key idea: R cot R_{\text{cot}} shapes text, R out R_{\text{out}} shapes computation. As pictured in fig. 2 , the key idea behind our framework is that R cot R_{\text{cot}} shapes the CoT text the model outputs, while R out R_{\text{out}} shapes the computation the model performs using that CoT. This is because R cot R_{\text{cot}} , by definition, depends only on the CoT text and is agnostic to the computational content of the CoT. Conversely, R out R_{\text{out}} depends on the final output and therefore shapes which computations the model carries out to reach that output. Issues for transparency arise when these two pressures diverge: R cot R_{\text{cot}} pushes the text in one direction while R out R_{\text{out}} pushes the computation in another.

sections.heading: 4 The Aligned / Orthogonal / In-Conflict Framework
sections.text: We now introduce the main contribution of our paper: a conceptual framework for reasoning about whether an RL environment will cause issues for CoT monitorability. 4.1 Definitions Figure 3 : Aligned, Orthogonal, and In-conflict rewards. We classify ( R cot , R out ) (R_{\text{cot}},R_{\text{out}}) pairs based on the relationship between CoT text which achieves a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} , and CoT computation which achieves a high R out R_{\text{out}} . In-Conflict : Punishing reward hacking means R cot R_{\text{cot}} leads to CoT text which does not talk about reward hacking, but CoT computations which lead to a high R out R_{\text{out}} do include text about reward hacking—this is incompatible. Orthogonal : The policy can easily express CoT text about reward hacking while speaking in all caps—CoT text with high R cot R_{\text{cot}} is compatible with expressing R out R_{\text{out}} computations. Aligned : Punishing incorrect reasoning allows the model to output fully correct code. By assumption, this achieves a higher R out R_{\text{out}} than the reward hacking strategy. This causes the model to transparently use the computations expressed in its CoT. CoT text with a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} causes computations that achieve a high R out R_{\text{out}} . We define our categories, which are based on reasoning about the properties of CoT text with high R cot R_{\text{cot}} and the properties of CoT computations with high R out R_{\text{out}} . These categories are pictured in fig. 3 . Core Assumption: Bias towards transparent CoT. Our definitions rest on the assumption that models have a strong inductive bias towards transparency due to pre-training on human language, so that absent strong optimization pressure, the CoT will remain transparent ( Brown-Cohen et al., 2026 , Appendix A.2) . This implies that if models can achieve a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} and a high R out R_{\text{out}} without sacrificing transparency, they will. In-conflict. A reward pair is in-conflict if CoT text which achieves a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} cannot describe the CoT computations which are needed to achieve a high R out R_{\text{out}} . Example: CoT monitor penalizing reward hacking. In the obfuscated reward hacking example, the CoT monitor penalizes the model when its CoT text mentions reward hacking, while R out R_{\text{out}} rewards hacking the unit tests. To achieve both, the model must output text that doesn’t mention reward hacking, while still using the CoT to compute reward-hacking actions. Claim: In-conflict rewards reduce transparency when optimized well. Once the model achieves high R cot R_{\text{cot}} , it can no longer transparently express the computations needed to achieve high R out R_{\text{out}} —hence it is incentivized to mask the computations in its CoT. This is what happens in the obfuscated reward hacking example. Orthogonal. A reward pair is orthogonal if there exists CoT text that both achieves high R cot R_{\text{cot}} and describes the CoT computations needed for high R out R_{\text{out}} . Example: Speak in all caps. Suppose R cot R_{\text{cot}} simply rewards the model for writing its CoT in all capital letters. The model can write “I WILL HACK THE UNIT TESTS” just as easily as “I will hack the unit tests”—the R cot R_{\text{cot}} constraint doesn’t prevent the model from transparently expressing its computations in its CoT text. Claim: Orthogonal rewards don’t affect transparency when optimized well. The model can achieve high R cot R_{\text{cot}} while still expressing the computations it needs for high R out R_{\text{out}} . Given our assumption that the model has a bias towards transparency, it will output CoT text that both achieves high R cot R_{\text{cot}} and transparently describes its computations. Aligned. A reward pair is aligned if CoT text that achieves a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} necessarily describes CoT computations that would improve R out R_{\text{out}} . Improvement is relative to a policy trained only on R out R_{\text{out}} . These are a subset of Orthogonal rewards. Example: Process supervision. In the obfuscated reward hacking example, suppose that: • R cot R_{\text{cot}} penalizes incorrect reasoning steps in the CoT text. • This reward allows the model to output CoT text corresponding to reasoning steps for a fully correct solution, instead of hacking the unit tests. • Without R cot R_{\text{cot}} the policy does not learn to do this—learning how to reason to correct solutions from R out R_{\text{out}} alone is too difficult. • The correct solution achieves an even higher R out R_{\text{out}} than the obfuscated reward hacking strategy, as some tests are not hackable. This is an example of an aligned pair of rewards: the CoT text which achieves a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} describes computations that lead to higher R out R_{\text{out}} than what the policy achieves when trained on R out R_{\text{out}} (where it resorts to reward hacking). Claim: Aligned rewards improve transparency when optimized well. In the aligned case, consider a model that begins with non-transparent reasoning, i.e. whose CoT computations are mismatched with the CoT text. Once the model achieves high R cot R_{\text{cot}} it is incentivized to switch to having the CoT computations match those described in the CoT text, as this would improve R out R_{\text{out}} , and is the default behavior of the model. In our example, a policy that begins with obfuscated reward hacking would, under process supervision, learn to output CoT text describing computations for a correct solution and then transition to have its CoT computations correspond to the CoT text. We regard the claims that aligned rewards improve transparency as more speculative, since (1) we do not test the claim empirically, and (2) these rewards cause large changes in the model’s CoT text, making unexpected effects more likely. Therefore, we urge caution for practitioners using CoT rewards that improve final output performance. 4.2 Training against in-conflict rewards may not always reduce transparency It is important to note that if a policy does not achieve high enough R cot R_{\text{cot}} and R out R_{\text{out}} performance, we will not see issues with transparency. For example, we could imagine a policy that reward hacks (high R out R_{\text{out}} ) while mentioning reward hacking in its CoT (low R cot R_{\text{cot}} ). Whether a particular training run becomes non-transparent therefore depends on the ability to optimize the in-conflict rewards, which could vary considerably in practice. Claim: In-conflict rewards are hard to optimize. Since we assume the policy has an inductive bias towards transparency, and in-conflict rewards are the only rewards that require overcoming this bias (by incentivizing non-transparent CoTs), we expect them to be harder to optimize than other reward types. We show empirical evidence for this claim in section 6.3 . 4.3 Monitorability Our definitions so far have all been centered around transparency —whether the CoT text describes the CoT computations. However, in the rest of the paper we measure monitorability —whether the CoT text helps a CoT monitor complete a downstream monitoring task (e.g., classify whether the policy is reward hacking). We connect these two concepts as follows: the monitor tries to classify an aspect of the CoT’s computation (e.g. whether it relates to reward hacking) by reading the CoT text. Monitorability is reduced whenever the CoT text is non-transparent with respect to the specific computations the monitor needs to detect. When considering classifying reward pairs as in-conflict with respect to some monitoring task, we still consider the set of CoT computations that are needed to achieve a high R out R_{\text{out}} , but we are only interested in the subset of those computations we need for our monitoring task. We say R cot R_{\text{cot}} is in conflict with respect to a monitoring task if CoT text achieving high R cot R_{\text{cot}} cannot describe the subset of CoT computations relevant to that task. This makes being in conflict with respect to a monitoring task a stronger condition than in the transparency case, and hence some reward pairs that were previously in-conflict can become orthogonal. For example, in the obfuscated reward hacking case, we can consider monitorability with respect to classifying whether the model is completing a coding task. Training against a CoT monitor for reward hacking is orthogonal with respect to this monitoring task—the CoT text can still express that the model is writing code without mentioning reward hacking specifically. We talk about this equivalence more precisely in appendix C .

sections.heading: 5 Applying the Framework
sections.text: We now introduce our RL environments and use the framework to classify each ( R cot , R out ) (R_{\text{cot}},R_{\text{out}}) pair. Importantly, all classifications were made before we ran any of the experiments presented in section 6 . 5.1 Base environments ( R out R_{\text{out}} ) Recall that our LLM policy π \pi maps a prompt p p to some CoT c c and a final output o o (i.e. π ⁡ ( p ) = ( c , o ) \pi(p)=(c,o) ). Our base environments are defined by a distribution over prompts and an R out R_{\text{out}} reward term. Our R out R_{\text{out}} takes in the model’s output o o and the input prompt p p and outputs a scalar between − 1 -1 and 1 1 . We consider two environments: 1. Heads-And-Tails : A simple state-tracking task taken from Skaf et al. (2025) , where models are asked to track the state of a coin over N N rounds of being or not being flipped. R out = 1 R_{\text{out}}=1 if the model’s final output is equal to the correct final state of the coin (“Heads” or “Tails”), and R out = 0 R_{\text{out}}=0 otherwise. Unless otherwise stated, we consider N = 6 N=6 flips. 2. Backdoor-Easy : A set of simple coding problems taken from a modified version of the Mostly Basic Python Programming Problems (MBPP) dataset ( Austin et al., 2021 ) . In this case, R out = 1 R_{\text{out}}=1 if the code is both (1) Correct (passes a set of held out unit tests), and (2) Backdoored (there is an input where the code’s output differs from a gold solution). This is a simplified version of the environment in Wagner et al. (2025) . See appendix D for precise prompts and implementation details. 5.2 Measuring monitorability To measure monitorability we need to define a monitoring task. The task we consider is whether a CoT monitor given only c c can correctly classify which type of task the model’s reasoning corresponds to: • In Heads-And-Tails , the monitor receives a score of 1 1 if it classifies the reasoning as being about a coin, and 0 0 otherwise. • In Backdoor-Easy , the monitor receives a score of 1 1 if it classifies the reasoning as involving a backdoor, and 0 0 otherwise. Both monitors are prompted LLMs, with prompts manually optimized on a set of example reasoning traces. 5.3 Classifying reward pairs We now describe the R cot R_{\text{cot}} reward terms we use across our environments—our R cot R_{\text{cot}} functions map from the model’s CoT c c and the prompt p p , to a scalar between -1 and 1. We classify each ( R cot , R out ) (R_{\text{cot}},R_{\text{out}}) pair using our framework. For rewards classified as in conflict, we separately consider whether they are in conflict with respect to transparency and with respect to our monitoring tasks. R cot R_{\text{cot}} \ R out R_{\text{out}} Heads & Tails Backdoor-easy Length Penalty In-conflict In-conflict CoT Monitor In-conflict In-conflict Human Prefs Orthogonal In-conflict Punish String Orthogonal Orthogonal Process Supervision Aligned N/A Table 1 : Classifications when applying our conceptual framework. Green = Aligned , Blue = Orthogonal , Red = In-conflict . All in-conflict rewards are in conflict with respect to both transparency and our monitoring tasks. CoT Monitor ( In-Conflict ). In Heads-And-Tails , R cot R_{\text{cot}} penalizes the model whenever the CoT text appears to involve reasoning about a coin; in Backdoor-Easy , it penalizes reasoning that involves a backdoor. This is in conflict when considering transparency, as CoT text which achieves a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} necessarily does not mention the CoT computations which achieve a high R out R_{\text{out}} (computations involving coins and backdoors). Furthermore, since our monitoring task involves classifying whether the model is reasoning about coins or backdoors, this is also in conflict with respect to monitorability. Length Penalty ( In-Conflict ). A penalty on generations which exceed a minimum threshold L min L_{\min} : R cot len ​ ( p , c ) = − max ⁡ ( 0 , | c | − L min ) R_{\text{cot}}^{\text{len}}(p,c)=-\max(0,|c|-L_{\min}) (1) where | c | |c| denotes length (in tokens or characters). We use the character-based variant in Heads-And-Tails and the token-based variant in Backdoor-Easy . Training with length penalties is in-conflict across all of our base environments, since very short reasoning cannot transparently express the CoT computations the model is using. More specifically, we assume that to achieve high R out R_{\text{out}} the CoT computation must contain some minimal set of reasoning steps—for example, in Heads-And-Tails this may be tracking N N flips of a coin. We can consider the set of all CoT text which would describe this minimal set of CoT computations, and consider the length of the shortest text in that set (call that length L min-transparent L_{\text{min-transparent}} ). If the LLM achieves high enough R cot R_{\text{cot}} that the length of its CoT is less than L min-transparent L_{\text{min-transparent}} , we know it cannot be transparently expressing the computations in its CoT. The same reasoning makes length penalty in-conflict for our monitorability definition—we can consider the set of text which describes the subset of CoT computations that we are monitoring. We believe that in Heads-And-Tails , token-based length penalties are likely still orthogonal for monitorability. Although sufficiently short CoT text may obscure important parts of the computation (and hence be in conflict for transparency), “Heads,” “Tails,” and “Coin” are each a single token. Hence CoT text which achieves a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} may still be orthogonal w.r.t. our monitors. We train against the character-based length penalty for Heads-And-Tails in section 6 , and classify that variant as in-conflict. Human Preferences ( In-Conflict or Orthogonal ). An LLM grader which is prompted to judge whether a human would like, be neutral toward, or dislike the CoT text, assigning R cot ∈ { + 1 , 0 , − 1 } R_{\text{cot}}\in\{+1,0,-1\} accordingly. Whether this is in conflict depends on R out R_{\text{out}} . In Heads-And-Tails , we expect that CoT text scoring high on R cot R_{\text{cot}} corresponds to clear, well-structured reasoning that can easily express the computations needed for high R out R_{\text{out}} ; hence this pair is orthogonal. In Backdoor-Easy , however, the grader is told the user wants a correct solution, so highly rated CoT text is unlikely to mention backdoors—yet backdoor-related computations are needed for high R out R_{\text{out}} , making this pair in conflict. Punish String ( Orthogonal ). A reward which punishes a specific set of strings being present in the CoT, i.e. R cot = − 1 R_{\text{cot}}=-1 if c c contains a (case-insensitive) match in some set of strings 𝒲 \mathcal{W} and R cot = 0 R_{\text{cot}}=0 otherwise. In Heads-And-Tails , 𝒲 = { heads , tails } \mathcal{W}=\{\texttt{heads},\texttt{tails}\} ; in the backdoor environments, 𝒲 = { backdoor } \mathcal{W}=\{\texttt{backdoor}\} . Punishing a specific string does not prevent the model from expressing the relevant semantics—the model can rephrase its CoT without mentioning that string while still expressing whatever computations R out R_{\text{out}} incentivizes (e.g., using a synonym or misspelling). Achieving high R cot R_{\text{cot}} therefore does not affect the model’s ability to transparently describe the computations needed for high R out R_{\text{out}} . Process Supervision ( Aligned ). An LLM grader returning R cot = − 1 R_{\text{cot}}=-1 if any of the reasoning steps in c c are are not making valid progress towards a correct answer, and R cot = 0 R_{\text{cot}}=0 otherwise. CoT text achieving a high R cot R_{\text{cot}} corresponds to valid reasoning for the task. If models trained only on R out R_{\text{out}} fail to complete the task this means that achieving high enough R cot R_{\text{cot}} leads to CoT text that describes CoT computations which would improve the model’s performance—making this reward function aligned. We only implement process supervision in Heads-And-Tails .

sections.heading: 6 Empirical Results
sections.text: For each of the reward function pairs described in section 5 , we run hyperparameter sweeps and select the policy that performed highest on R cot + R out R_{\text{cot}}+R_{\text{out}} across our sweep. We then evaluate the monitorability of these highly performing policies, and compare with the predictions from our theoretical framework. Our two main findings are: (1) our conceptual classification is predictive of monitorability issues, and (2) in-conflict rewards are consistently harder to optimize than orthogonal or aligned ones. 6.1 Learning algorithms With the aim of demonstrating our framework’s generality, we optimize LLM policies against our rewards using two different learning algorithms: GRPO with token-level rewards (CAPO). Standard GRPO assigns the same reward to all tokens in a sequence. We use a modified version of GRPO ( Xie et al., 2025 , CAPO;) that allows us to assign rewards on a per-token basis. Credit assignment is done either by prompting the CoT monitor to identify which tokens were most relevant to a reward decision, or programmatically (e.g. matching the tokens that contain a punished string). We found token-level credit assignment to be necessary for several of our reward pairs to optimize effectively. For example, in Heads-And-Tails , our process supervision reward punishes specific incorrect reasoning steps rather than the entire sequence. We present results for Qwen-3-14B in this section, with Gemma-3 results in appendix E . In-Context RL (ICRL). We also make use of an in-context RL algorithm ( Moeini et al., 2025 ) using Claude Opus 4.5 as the policy model. ICRL iteratively optimizes the agent’s behavior against a reward by prompting the model with previous trajectories that received high reward. See appendix I for details. For example model completions, see appendix F . Figure 4 : A & B: Empirical monitorability scores match framework predictions. We measure the monitorability of policies trained with different R cot R_{\text{cot}} rewards across our two environments. Bar colors indicate the theoretical classification of each reward pair: In-conflict , Orthogonal , Aligned . Solid bars show token-level RL results; hatched bars show in-context RL results. As predicted by our framework, in-conflict rewards lead to near-zero monitorability, while orthogonal and aligned rewards preserve high monitorability. C & D: In-conflict rewards are harder to learn. We compare the proportion of runs that achieve a score of > 0.8 >0.8 on both R cot R_{\text{cot}} and R out R_{\text{out}} across our training runs—we see that it is rarer for in-conflict rewards to be successfully optimized. Training curves (top) and representative completions (bottom) for two in-conflict reward pairs. Left: The length penalty compresses coin-tracking reasoning into terse arrow notation that a monitor cannot parse. Right: The CoT monitor causes the model to produce plausible reasoning that doesn’t mention a backdoor, while the output code still contains a backdoor. For full completions and training curves see appendices F and E . 6.2 Our framework is predictive Our classification was predictive of monitorability outcomes. As summarized in fig. 4 , our a priori classifications correctly predict monitorability across both Heads-And-Tails and Backdoor-Easy : in-conflict rewards lead to near-zero monitorability, while orthogonal and aligned rewards preserve it. We show representative in-conflict training curves and completions in fig. 5 . Aligned rewards improved performance in Heads-And-Tails . As shown in fig. 6 , when considering N = 42 N=42 flips, a policy trained only on R out R_{\text{out}} achieves random performance. Our aligned R cot R_{\text{cot}} improves R out R_{\text{out}} performance relative to this baseline. As shown in fig. 4 , this also did not affect monitorability. Note that we could not test the framework’s prediction that these rewards actively improve monitorability, since monitorability is already perfect at the start of training in our setting. Length penalty caused only trivial unmonitorability in Backdoor-Easy . For the setting where we see consistent monitorability drops, the behavior is trivial—the policy simply outputs empty reasoning. See completions and training curves in appendix F . We observe “semantic drift” in ICRL. As described in section I.7 , we see prompt-dependent semantic drift in ICRL on Heads-And-Tails : models slowly drop in monitorability when training against some orthogonal rewards with certain prompts, even though this does not help reward performance. This fits the dynamic hypothesized by Schoen et al. (2025) , which our framework does not capture. Figure 6 : Process supervision is aligned in Heads-And-Tails . Our aligned rewards improve outcome performance while not hurting monitorability. Unlike the other experiments, which consider N = 6 N=6 flips, we track N = 42 N=42 flips. 6.3 In-conflict rewards are difficult to optimize A key secondary finding is that in-conflict rewards are harder to optimize than orthogonal or aligned ones. This is consistent with the claim that models have an inductive bias towards transparent reasoning ( section 4 ), and corroborates similar observations in Wagner et al. (2025) ; Skaf et al. (2025) ; MacDermott et al. (2025) . It is generally hard to prove a negative (i.e. “X cannot be learned”), but we provide several lines of circumstantial evidence for this claim. Learning often fails with in-conflict reward pairs. Figure 4 shows that the proportion of seeds achieving high scores on both R cot R_{\text{cot}} and R out R_{\text{out}} is substantially lower for in-conflict rewards than for other reward types. Furthermore, all of our Gemma optimization failures were against in-conflict rewards (see appendix E ). Qualitatively, in-conflict rewards required much more iteration. Throughout the project, learning against in-conflict rewards was unstable and required substantially more hyperparameter tuning, whereas orthogonal and aligned rewards often worked immediately. We switched to token-level rewards (CAPO) after standard GRPO failed to optimize in-conflict reward pairs, and we remained in toy environments largely because of the difficulty of learning against in-conflict rewards in more complex settings.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations & Future Work
sections.text: More realistic and diverse training environments. Our environments are relatively simple, and hence perhaps our empirical results do not generalize to real LLM post-training. Future work should run similar experiments on training distributions that are closer to production LLM RL training. Methods for predicting failures of optimization. As described in section 5 , whether we see monitorability problems depends on the policy getting high enough performance on both R cot R_{\text{cot}} and R out R_{\text{out}} . It is difficult to know what level of performance is likely to cause issues in practice. Hence, whether a drop in monitorability will actually be observed is unclear. For example, many modern models are trained with length penalties without any observed drop in monitorability ( Guan et al., 2025 ) . Empirically detecting aligned / orthogonal / in-conflict. Although we think that our framework is conceptually useful, we expect in many cases it may be unclear which category a pair of rewards falls into—hence, turning this into something we can measure empirically would be valuable. Transparency “drift”. Chain-of-Thought semantics might change during long training runs even without concrete incentives. Schoen et al. (2025) hypothesize that this effect occurs in some state-of-the-art reasoning models. We observed such a semantics “drift” in one of our in-context RL experiments as a result of a prompt that encouraged the policy model to improve the reward even after the highest possible reward was achieved (cf. section I.7 ). Studying this effect is an interesting direction for future work.
